sources.title: CARISMA: CAR-Integrated Service Mesh Architecture
sources.role: Author paper used to verify the multi-HPC service-mesh architecture, proof-of-concept setup, runtime relocation behavior, and evaluation boundary.

claims.text: CARISMA adapts the service-mesh pattern to multiple interlinked automotive HPCs, with a central Control Plane, one proxy per HPC, node/service registries, and location-transparent service routing.
The architecture can model a cloud backend as another registered node/service endpoint so in-vehicle callers use the same proxy-mediated service mechanism.
claims.context: Architecture capability described by the authors.

claims.text: A proof of concept on two private-networked virtual machines used Go, gRPC, Envoy, a Control Plane, registries, orchestrator and three software components; the authors demonstrated communication across nodes and relocation of a service without reconfiguring its caller.

limitations.text: Validation is a two-VM proof of concept rather than embedded automotive HPC hardware or an in-vehicle network.
The authors explicitly defer a sound evaluation of CARISMA overhead versus direct inter-service communication to future work.
The prototype intentionally uses exactly one proxy per HPC and does not claim redundant proxy behavior.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for CARISMA: CAR-Integrated Service Mesh Architecture; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The primary paper establishes the multi-HPC service-mesh design and a two-VM proof-of-concept feasibility test, while explicitly leaving communication-overhead evaluation for future work.

unresolved_questions: What latency, jitter, CPU/memory overhead and failure-mode behavior would CARISMA exhibit on automotive HPC hardware and deterministic in-vehicle networks?

editorial.why_now_note: CARISMA directly explores the runtime/service-routing consequences of distributing software across multiple automotive HPCs, a central issue in centralized/zonal SDV architectures.
editorial.rationale: Strong architecture-pattern evidence for separating service location from application logic, with clear prototype limitations that can be carried into comparison.
